sub_sections.title: Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages
sub_sections.content:
WP Number: 1

WP title: Trustworthy, Explainable and Causal AI Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary A

Participants Academic Beneficiaries B, C, D, E

DCs involved 1,2,4,6,8

Objectives: This WP will ensure that AI models are transparent, interpretable and able to quantify uncertainty, thereby enhancing trustworthiness and supporting compliance with applicable governance requirements in operational settings.

Task 1.1 - Fairness analysis of state-of-the-art AI models in specific populations: Underrepresented groups are often insufficiently represented in training data, leading to dataset shifts and performance disparities. We will perform a detailed fairness analysis of advanced AI models for decision-support applications. This includes identifying proxy variables encoding sensitive attributes through explainability methods and validating results using composite metrics balancing fairness and performance. This task will establish baseline benchmarks for subsequent developments.

Task 1.2 – Model Explainability and Interpretability: Develop population-level explainability methods for multimodal data by creating unbiased and generalisable interpretability frameworks for safety-critical decision support. We will quantify modality contributions and assess feature relevance through attribution methods combined with counterfactual explanations.

Task 1.3 – Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis: Analyse sensitivity and quantify uncertainty in multimodal AI systems. Integrate uncertainty estimates into user-facing outputs to support safe human oversight and to identify unfamiliar populations, environments or operating conditions.

Task 1.4 – Causality in Multimodal AI: Investigate causal relationships and confounding variables that may influence both interventions and outcomes. Develop causal modelling approaches capable of improving robustness, transparency and interpretability in complex multimodal environments.

WP Number: 2

WP title: Interoperable, Robust and Privacy-Preserving AI Systems Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary F

Participants Academic Beneficiaries C, G, A

DCs involved 1,2,3,5,9

Objectives: The aim is to develop interoperable, privacy-preserving, robust and knowledge-aware AI systems that comply with regulatory requirements and integrate into operational information infrastructures.

Task 2.1 – Integration of Multimodal Information: Develop machine-learning methods to integrate heterogeneous data sources for improved prediction, classification and risk assessment. Multimodal fusion architectures, temporal models, harmonisation strategies and augmentation pipelines will be investigated. Causal reasoning methods will be combined with advanced representation-learning approaches to generate interpretable outputs.

Task 2.2 – Robust and Knowledge-Augmented Learning: Improve robustness and generalisability across heterogeneous datasets by integrating formalised domain knowledge into learning architectures. Beyond model-agnostic approaches, we will develop knowledge-aware models that embed mathematical, logical and causal relations while reducing complexity and improving interpretability.

Task 2.3 – Privacy-Preserving AI Models: Develop and evaluate privacy-preserving machine-learning methods for embedded and distributed environments. Implement distributed learning approaches combining local processing and centralised inference while minimising data exposure. Evaluate privacy, resource efficiency and performance trade-offs, and develop privacy-by-design recommendations aligned with applicable regulations.

Task 2.4 – Data, Processing and Model Interoperability: Identify, evaluate and select interoperability standards for data, models and processing environments. This includes semantic and syntactic metadata standards, secure communication protocols, privacy assessments and deployment requirements. Interoperability gaps will be identified together with developers, users and governance stakeholders.

WP Number: 3

WP title: Human-AI Collaboration Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary B

Participants Academic Beneficiaries H, I, F

DCs involved 3,4,6,7,9

Objectives: This WP builds trust through human-in-the-loop approaches, providing users with tools to validate and refine AI outputs while ensuring usability, co-creation and alignment with real-world workflows and societal requirements.

Task 3.1 – Establishment of Human-in-the-Loop Paradigms: Co-create human-in-the-loop models enabling users to explore outputs, provide feedback and make corrections. Develop scalable solutions for individual-level and population-level assessments, evaluate workflow integration, and assess usability, reliability and trust. Explainability methods will be integrated in collaboration with WP1.

Task 3.2 – Human-AI Collaboration for Professional End Users: Co-create improved methods for presenting AI outputs to domain experts, focusing on relevance, clarity and integration into decision-making workflows. The resulting communication strategies will be validated in representative operational environments.

Task 3.3 – Human-AI Collaboration Through Monitoring Dashboards: Review existing approaches for monitoring trustworthy decision-support systems, define a design framework and co-design a population-level monitoring dashboard. Validation activities will assess accuracy, workflow integration and organisational impact.

Task 3.4 – Human-AI Collaboration for End Users and Stakeholders: Co-create approaches for communicating AI outputs to non-specialist users in order to improve transparency, trust, autonomy and engagement. AI predictions, risks and uncertainties will be translated into understandable and actionable information.

WP Number: 4 WP title: Clinical Adaptation & Case Studies Start month - End month: M1-M36 Lead participant Academic Beneﬁciary E Participants Academic Beneﬁciaries I, F, G, B, C DCs involved 3,5,6,7,8,9 Objectives To adapt, validate and evaluate trustworthy AI models in clinically relevant settings using retrospective and implementation-oriented studies covering cardiovascular medicine, neurodegenerative disease, critical care and medical-device environments.

Task 4.0 – AI Implementation in Clinical Practice

Identify barriers to healthcare AI adoption and establish a shared understanding of implementation requirements across participating healthcare environments.

Activities include:

• workflow analysis,

• stakeholder engagement,

• implementation-readiness assessment,

• shadow-mode deployment planning,

• impact assessment for future clinical adoption.

Evaluation focuses on diagnostic quality, workflow efficiency, trust and usability.

Task 4.1 – Federated Learning Infrastructure Across Clinical Sites

Expand federated-learning capabilities across participating clinical environments to enable privacy-preserving training and evaluation without centralising sensitive patient data.

Activities include:

• federated infrastructure deployment,

• interoperability testing,

• distributed model evaluation,

• multicentre validation.

Task 4.2 – AI Implementation for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)

Retrospective evaluation of multimodal causal AI models using:

• ECG,

• EMG,

• echocardiography,

• biomarkers,

• longitudinal clinical records.

Primary objectives:

• progression prediction,

• survival prediction,

• causal discovery across neurocardiological biomarkers.

The task investigates links between cardiac biomarkers, neuromuscular status and disease progression while developing interpretable prognostic tools for multidisciplinary ALS care.

Task 4.3 – AI Implementation for Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI)

Retrospective multicentre evaluation of multimodal causal AI models in structural heart disease.

Data sources include:

• cardiac CT,

• ECG,

• demographic variables,

• procedural characteristics,

• mortality outcomes,

• pacemaker implantation outcomes.

Objectives include:

• intervention-risk prediction,

• identification of treatment-outcome confounding,

• multicentre validation,

• federated-learning evaluation.

Task 4.4 – AI Implementation for Heart Failure and Wearable Biosignal Data

Evaluate AI systems using longitudinal healthcare pathways that integrate workplace and remote monitoring data.

Data types include:

• smartwatch biosignals,

• ambulatory recordings,

• hospital measurements,

• longitudinal clinical outcomes.

Primary applications include:

• rehospitalisation prediction,

• mortality risk prediction,

• chronic heart-failure management,

• long-term monitoring support.

Task 4.5 – AI Implementation for Critical-Care and Population-Based Case Studies

Adapt and evaluate multimodal AI models using large-scale critical-care datasets.

Target applications include:

• early detection of acute cardiac dysfunction,

• arrhythmia prediction,

• cardiac-arrest prediction,

• mortality-risk assessment,

• intensive-care decision support.

Validation is conducted using large publicly available critical-care datasets and multicentre healthcare records.

Task 4.6 – AI Translation Into Industrial Healthcare Applications

Transfer methods developed in earlier work packages into industrial medical-device environments.

Two primary demonstrators are maintained:

A. Long-Term EEG Technologies

Transfer explainable and causal AI methodologies developed for cardiovascular biosignals toward:

• seizure classification,

• seizure prediction,

• long-term wearable EEG monitoring,

• neurophysiological decision support.

B. Contactless Neonatal Monitoring

Transfer privacy-preserving AI architectures into:

• neonatal incubator environments,

• contactless vital-sign monitoring,

• camera-based physiological sensing.

This includes validation of distributed AI methods in regulated medical-device development workflows.

WP Number: 5

WP title: Coordination and management Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary A

Participants All beneficiaries

DCs involved –

Objectives: To ensure effective coordination and governance of the Doctoral Network. This WP covers project management, monitoring progress and risks, financial and administrative coordination.

Task 5.1 – Project Management: Oversee the consortium’s scientific, administrative, and financial management, including consortium agreements. Monitor deliverables, milestones, risks, and ethics compliance. Report to the funding authority and ensure alignment with programme framework requirements. Chair the steering and supervisory boards.

Task 5.2 – Quality Assurance and Risk Management: Implement monitoring mechanisms for the progress of work packages and doctoral candidates. Establish risk management procedures, ensure compliance with regulations, and institutional ethical requirements.

WP Number: 6

WP title: Training and Career Development Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary D

Participants

All beneficiaries

DCs involved DC1-9

Objectives: Implementation of an impactful training programme at the interfaces of AI, application domain expertise, and education to enhance PhD career prospects and skills development. Monitoring progress toward training goals TG1–6 (see Sec. 1.3.2).

Task 6.1 – Career development plan: Set-up of personal career development plan (PCDP, see e.g., Section 1.4) for each researcher plus a comprehensive list of them (all beneficiaries including annual updates).

Task 6.2 – PhD committee: Establishment and implementation of a PhD committee (see Section 2.2) for all DCs comprising supervisors from academia, the non-academic sector, and associated partners (secondment).

Task 6.3 – Training progress monitoring: Organisation of training events including quality and needs monitoring via feedback mechanism (Supervisory Board).

WP Number: 7

WP title: Impact and Innovation Start month – End month: M1 – M36

Lead participant Academic Beneficiary H

Participants Academic Beneficiary A

DCs involved DC1-9

Objectives: Efficient, timely, relevant impact of the project’s outcomes on scientific, technological, innovative and societal levels. Implementation of mechanisms to ensure longevity and sustainability of the created outputs.

Task 7.1 – Communication and Impact Strategy (Academic Beneficiaries H, A): Development and annual update of a strategy for targeted dissemination, exploitation and communication including progress monitoring. Set-up of appropriate external communication channels, webpages, and a knowledge hub, as well as organizing roundtables and minisymposia at international conferences and workshops.

Task 7.2 – Knowledge Transfer (Academic Beneficiary H): Transform research outcomes into innovations, guidelines, and policy inputs through structured exploitation measures. Develop and apply a Research-to-Innovation (R2I) Canvas to map the scientific, technological, and societal value of each DC’s work and ensure early alignment with industrial needs and policy priorities.

Task 7.3 – Post-project exploitation (Academic Beneficiary H): Develop a follow-up research strategy to foster future collaboration by identifying funding opportunities related to mobility, staff exchanges, and networking. This will support scientific collaboration and identify relevant future programme calls for continued joint research activities.

sub_sections.title: Quality, capacity and role of each participant, including hosting arrangements and extent to which the consortium as a whole brings together the necessary expertise (Sanitized)
sub_sections.content:
Appropriateness of the infrastructure and capacity of each participating organisation, in light of the tasks allocated to them in the action

The Doctoral Network is supported by a tightly integrated ecosystem of AI, data and clinical infrastructures, fully aligned with the WPs and DC projects. Across the consortium, technical universities, comprehensive universities and academic medical centres contribute complementary, task-aligned facilities.

• HPC clusters and AI labs (Academic Beneficiaries A, B, C, H): GPU clusters, dataflow systems and specialised ML/DL/causal-inference toolchains supporting AI model development in WP1.

• National-scale AI infrastructures (Academic Beneficiary C): access to large- scale computational resources, AI-driven services and datasets, enabling multimodal health-data research in WP2.

• Secure medical-data and interoperability infrastructures (Academic Beneficiaries E, G): secure clinical data facilities and AI pipelines for clinical training and inference in WP2.

• Clinical registries and biobanks (Academic Beneficiary I): multimodal registries and biobanks combining clinical, biomarker, biosignal and imaging data, plus advanced electrophysiology, imaging and neurophysiology facilities supporting WP3–4 use cases.

• Biomedical measurement and monitoring laboratories (Academic Beneficiary H): contactless physiological monitoring platforms, simulation environments and multimodal physiological setups supporting privacy- preserving sensing research in WP2.

• Digital-health, next-generation connectivity and HCI testbeds (Academic Beneficiary F): campus-wide advanced networking infrastructure, field-testing environments and user-centred digital-health research facilities supporting WP3.

• Open-access life-science core facilities: sequencing, flow cytometry, proteomics, structural biology, advanced imaging and biocomputing resources supporting WP4 and providing insight into multi-omics and biomarker pipelines linked to target health applications.

All DCs are embedded in accredited doctoral schools and established research groups with clear hosting arrangements. International offices support housing, integration, language learning and practical mobility aspects.

Consortium composition and exploitation of participating organisations' complementarities

The consortium covers the full innovation chain of trustworthy causal AI in health through deliberate complementarities.

Methodological depth at Academic Beneficiaries A, B, C, F and H spans biomedical signal and image processing, causal and explainable AI, medical imaging and digital- health software engineering.

Clinical and data breadth at Academic Beneficiaries E, G and I includes cardiovascular medicine, electrophysiology, neurology and rare-disease applications.

Academic Beneficiaries G and H contribute regulatory and interoperability expertise, including privacy-preserving AI, data-protection standards and compliance with major European regulatory frameworks.

Academic Beneficiary F strengthens the consortium with leading digital-health and human-technology-interaction capacities.

These complementarities are embedded in the network’s design: each DC project combines at least two environments through co-supervision and international/intersectoral secondments.

Foundational AI outputs flow into infrastructure and deployment activities and then into clinical and digital-health pilots, such as prognostic modelling, intervention-risk modelling and physiological-monitoring applications.

Furthermore, cross-cutting training in open science, ethics, regulation and innovation enables DCs to link technical advances with clinical, legal and implementation needs.

Role of associated partners to the programme

Associated partners strengthen the network with specialised causal-AI expertise, industrial translation capacity and broader clinical validation.

Non-academic Beneficiary D contributes advanced causal and explainable AI expertise and model uncertainty quantification competence, co-supervising DCs and providing access to specialised development environments and datasets.

Industrial Partners A, B and C provide quality-managed development environments, regulatory expertise and facilities for integrating trustworthy AI into real-world products during DC secondments.

Additional associated academic and clinical partners contribute complementary patient cohorts, datasets and care settings for external validation and for human-in-the- loop co-creation.

They are fully integrated into supervision, training and governance, co-supervising DCs, hosting secondments and contributing to network schools, workshops and advisory structures to ensure that scientific advances align with clinical needs and industrial feasibility.

sub_sections.title: Recruitment strategy (including how the project will strive to adhere to the Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers) (Sanitized)
sub_sections.content:
The Doctoral Network implements a unified, open and merit-based recruitment procedure that adheres fully to the principles of the European Code of Conduct for the Recruitment of Researchers. Coordinated centrally under Work Package 5, recruitment is overseen by a Recruitment Manager and institutional HR departments to ensure that all doctoral candidates are selected through a transparent, inclusive and internationally comparable process.

All DC positions will be advertised simultaneously on EURAXESS, institutional channels and international scientific networks, with additional dissemination through communities supporting women and underrepresented groups in STEM. Advertisements will be written in inclusive language, present the roles broadly enough to attract diverse applicants, and describe working conditions, supervision arrangements, training opportunities and mobility requirements. Applications will be collected through institutional HR portals to guarantee GDPR-compliant handling. Calls will remain open for at least one month, with deadline extensions and reinforced outreach if the applicant pool lacks gender balance or sufficient qualified candidates.

Evaluation follows a structured and harmonised procedure. Each DC position is assessed by a Selection Committee made up of the main supervisor, a co-supervisor or expert from another partner institution and an HR representative. Committees aim for gender balance and intersectoral representation, ensuring broad expertise and fair evaluation. After eligibility checks, candidates are scored using shared criteria covering academic excellence, research potential, motivation and fit with the network’s interdisciplinary goals. Shortlisted candidates are interviewed online, and committees record decisions in a standardised selection report verified by the Recruitment Manager. All applicants receive outcome notifications, including brief feedback for those not selected.

The network embeds gender equality and diversity in recruitment by monitoring gender distribution in applications, longlists and shortlists. If imbalances arise, the Recruitment Manager triggers additional measures such as broader outreach, extended deadlines or targeted communication. Where feasible, anonymised initial screening will be used to minimise unconscious bias. Recruitment outputs are documented transparently in the Management Handbook and subject to oversight by the Supervisory Board. If a position remains unfilled, the consortium reassesses the advertisement and dissemination strategy, republishes the call with improved targeting and, if needed, adjusts timing or secondment planning. These steps follow established MSCA guidance that unsuccessful recruitment rounds require prompt corrective action.

The recruitment timeline is designed for coordination and clarity. All calls will be launched at project start, the application window will run for at least one month, evaluation and interviews will follow immediately, and appointments are expected between months four and six. This harmonised process ensures a fair, coherent and internationally comparable selection procedure that attracts excellent candidates and provides a solid foundation for the network’s research and training goals.

sub_sections.title: Network organisation (Fully Sanitized)
sub_sections.content:
The Doctoral Network is organised through a transparent governance structure integrating scientific leadership, training, impact and sustainability. The key bodies are the Project Coordinator and Management Team, the Supervisory Board (SB), the Dissemination, Exploitation and Communication (DEC) Committee, and the Innovation and Sustainability Committee. Together, these bodies ensure coherent implementation of the research and training programme, systematic monitoring of progress and risks, and alignment with applicable programme rules and project- management requirements. Detailed procedures (e.g. voting rules and escalation mechanisms) are defined in the Consortium Agreement and Management Handbook.

Project Coordinator and Management Team

The Coordinating Beneficiary is responsible for overall scientific, administrative and financial coordination of the Doctoral Network under Work Package 5 ("Coordination and Management"). Supported by project-management staff, the Coordinator:

• Monitors deliverables, milestones, risks and compliance activities across all work packages.

• Ensures timely scientific and financial reporting.

• Organises consortium and review meetings.

• Acts as the main interface between beneficiaries, associated partners and the funding authority.

The Project Manager maintains communication platforms and shared repositories, follows recruitment and secondments, collects reporting inputs and prepares meetings of governance bodies. This support enables supervisors and work-package leaders to focus on research, training and supervision activities while ensuring consistent implementation across institutions.

Supervisory Board (SB)

The Supervisory Board is the principal strategic body for research, training and supervision. It includes one representative from each beneficiary and selected associated partners, ensuring academic, clinical and industrial perspectives are represented.

The SB is responsible for:

• Overseeing the scientific direction and coherence of the research programme.

• Monitoring supervision quality and training implementation, including Individual Training Panels (ITPs), PhD Committees and Personal Career Development Plans (PCDPs).

• Reviewing progress reports and training feedback and proposing corrective measures where necessary.

• Ensuring recruitment, mobility and supervision respect researcher-charter principles as well as equality, diversity and inclusion policies.

The SB meets at least twice per year and may convene additional meetings when strategic decisions are required. Doctoral Candidate representatives may participate in discussions relating to training quality, wellbeing and career development.

Dissemination, Exploitation and Communication (DEC) Committee

The DEC Committee is the specialised body responsible for impact-related activities. It includes representatives from academic, clinical, industrial and regulatory sectors together with a doctoral-candidate representative.

Its responsibilities include:

• Designing and annually updating the dissemination, exploitation and communication strategy.

• Coordinating impact activities with Work Package 7.

• Defining and monitoring key performance indicators, including publications, software releases, policy outputs and outreach activities.

• Coordinating external communication channels such as websites, social media, workshops and conference events.

Within the DEC governance structure, an IP and Exploitation Panel reviews invention disclosures, advises on licensing and innovation opportunities and ensures that intellectual-property management remains aligned with consortium agreements and programme requirements.

The DEC Committee reports regularly to the Supervisory Board and recommends corrective measures whenever impact indicators require improvement.

Innovation and Sustainability Committee

The Innovation and Sustainability Committee focuses on sustaining impact beyond the project lifetime. It works closely with the Supervisory Board, DEC Committee and relevant work packages to:

• Monitor indicators of long-term collaboration and innovation.

• Support integration of successful training modules into local doctoral curricula.

• Coordinate development of follow-up research and training proposals.

• Ensure sustainability considerations are incorporated into planning and governance.

The Committee supports the long-term sustainability of project outputs, training resources and collaborative structures established by the Doctoral Network.

Monitoring, Decision-Making and Internal Communication

Monitoring and decision-making processes are embedded throughout the governance structure:

• Work Package leaders submit regular progress updates to the Coordinator and Project Manager.

• Training and supervision progress are monitored through annual reports and PCDP reviews.

• Impact indicators and intellectual-property matters are reviewed through the DEC structure and escalated where strategic decisions are required.

Internal communication is supported through:

• Regular virtual meetings.

• Mailing lists.

• Shared collaboration platforms.

• Internal document repositories.

At least one annual network-wide meeting brings together beneficiaries, associated partners and doctoral candidates, typically aligned with major training events to optimise efficiency.

Internal Communication Strategy

The consortium maintains:

• Shared intranet and document repositories.

• Project-wide mailing lists.

• Standard video-conferencing channels.

The Supervisory Board reviews scientific progress, training, risks and finances on a regular basis. Work Package leaders organise online coordination meetings, supported by dedicated communication channels for doctoral candidates. All formal meetings generate concise, action-oriented minutes stored in shared repositories.

Financial Management Strategy

Financial management is embedded within Work Package 5 and governed by the Grant Agreement and Consortium Agreement.

The Coordinating Beneficiary:

• Receives and distributes project funding according to the agreed budget.

• Monitors expenditure across work packages and doctoral-candidate positions.

• Oversees annual internal financial reporting.

Each beneficiary manages the resources associated with its own doctoral candidates and project activities. Where doctoral programmes extend beyond the funded period, institutions may provide complementary resources to support successful completion of doctoral training.

Gender Equality and Diversity in Network Organisation

Gender equality and diversity principles are embedded throughout the governance structure.

The consortium will:

• Strive for balanced representation within governance bodies.

• Consider diversity in committee membership, leadership positions and invited speakers.

• Monitor participation and representation indicators using anonymised and legally compliant statistics.

• Review these indicators regularly and implement corrective actions when persistent imbalances are identified.

Governance bodies may therefore introduce targeted measures to strengthen representation and visibility of underrepresented groups where appropriate.

sub_sections.title: Ethics Self-Assessment (Sanitized)
sub_sections.content:
The project develops trustworthy, causal AI for healthcare applications using retrospective clinical data and limited prospective human-factors studies.

All activities will:

• Follow applicable ethical principles, international standards and national regulations.

• Involve voluntary participation with informed consent where required.

• Exclude activities involving embryos, embryonic stem cells, human tissues, animal experimentation or other sensitive biological research areas.

The principal ethical risks relate to:

• Privacy and data protection.

• Potential re-identification of individuals.

• Bias in datasets, algorithms or outcomes.

• Misinterpretation of AI-generated outputs.

These risks will be mitigated through:

• Pseudonymisation and privacy-preserving data-management approaches.

• Secure processing environments.

• Transparent communication regarding model limitations.

• Appropriate human oversight throughout development, validation and deployment.

AI development follows an ethics-by-design approach aligned with applicable data- protection, medical-device and AI-governance frameworks. Fairness, transparency, robustness and bias-mitigation measures are embedded throughout model design and evaluation. Federated and privacy-preserving methodologies are used where appropriate to minimise unnecessary data movement.

For any international collaboration, all data-related activities will comply with relevant legal requirements governing cross-border data transfers.

All activities involving human participants, personal data or clinical information will commence only after the required ethical, regulatory and data-protection approvals have been obtained, ensuring protection of participants’ rights, dignity and safety throughout the project.

The project will comply with the highest ethical standards and with applicable international, European and national legislation concerning:

• Data protection and privacy.

• Research integrity.

• Clinical research.

• Medical technologies.

• Artificial-intelligence governance.

• Health-data governance frameworks applicable during the project lifetime.

Compliance activities will be monitored continuously throughout the project to ensure that scientific excellence is achieved while maintaining ethical, legal and societal responsibility.

sub_sections.title: Environmental aspects in light of the MSCA Green Charter (Sanitized)
sub_sections.content:
The project will implement its research and training in line with the principles of the MSCA Green Charter, encouraging sustainable thinking in research management and day-to-day project practice. The consortium’s direct environmental footprint is moderate, as activities primarily involve computational research and collaboration rather than laboratory-intensive work. Environmental measures therefore focus on:

1. Responsible research and computing.

2. Awareness and training.

3. Sustainable organisation of activities.

Environmentally responsible research and computing

Partners will prioritise compact and energy-efficient computational approaches, careful experimental design and extensive code and data sharing to avoid unnecessary retraining and duplication of work.

Where possible:

• Computation-intensive tasks will be carried out using institutional or national computing infrastructures that follow sustainability or renewable-energy strategies.

• Software, datasets and teaching materials will be openly shared to maximise reuse and avoid unnecessary repetition of development efforts.

• Any equipment purchases will, where feasible, follow institutional green- procurement policies and prioritise durable and energy-efficient solutions.

Awareness and training for doctoral candidates and supervisors

Environmental sustainability will be integrated into the transferable-skills programme.

At least one network-wide training event will include topics such as:

• Environmental impacts of AI and digital-health technologies.

• Energy consumption associated with model training, storage and digital services.

• Hardware life-cycle considerations.

• Practical approaches to energy-efficient computing, including profiling, optimisation and resource-aware scheduling.

Doctoral candidates will be encouraged to consider environmental factors in their Personal Career Development Plans, including travel choices, remote collaboration practices and use of shared resources.

Supervisors and principal investigators will also receive guidance on the principles of the MSCA Green Charter to ensure alignment across partner institutions.

Sustainable organisation of project activities and events

Network meetings, training events and secondments will be organised to minimise travel-related emissions and waste while preserving the benefits of in-person interaction.

Measures include:

• Conducting routine meetings of governance bodies and work packages primarily online.

• Clustering in-person events where possible to reduce travel frequency.

• Organising major meetings in locations accessible through lower-emission transport options.

• Preferring venues with recognised sustainability policies or environmental certifications.

These measures aim to balance scientific collaboration with environmentally responsible project implementation.
